lesson.text: Quick memory: in a fair test, how many things do you change? (Just one, and keep everything else the same.) Designers test their ideas fairly too.
Designers make things for people. A design brief says who it is for and what it must do: 'Make a bag that can carry a lunchbox for a child of 8.'
The design cycle has five steps: idea, plan, make, test, improve. Then round again, until the design works well.
Idea and plan: think of many ideas, choose the best one, then draw it. Label the parts, the sizes, the materials and the tools you will need.
Make: measure twice and cut once. Mark your lines, cut carefully, and join the parts with glue, tape, string or stitches.
Test: does it do what the brief asked? Check each point: does it hold the lunchbox, is it easy to carry? A first model to test is called a prototype.
Improve: find what did not work, change it, and test again. Every designer's first try has problems: that is how designs get better.
Try it in the world: design a bridge across a river. Plan it on paper, build it, test it by walking across with a friend, then improve it and test it again.

exercises.prompt: Put the design cycle in order.
exercises.hint: You cannot test something before you make it.
exercises.explain: Idea, plan, make, test, improve: then round again.

exercises.hint: It comes at the very start.
choices: what it must do, and who it is for
exercises.explain: A design brief says who the product is for and what it must do.

exercises.prompt: Designers often need to improve their first model.
exercises.hint: Does every first try work perfectly?
exercises.explain: True: testing shows problems, and improving them makes the design better.

exercises.hint: It is made before the final version.
exercises.explain: A prototype is a first model, made so it can be tested and improved.

exercises.prompt: Which step comes straight after testing?
exercises.hint: What do you do when a test shows a problem?
exercises.explain: After testing comes improving: fix what did not work.

exercises.prompt: Which is a good rule for a lunch bag's design?
exercises.hint: What must the bag do for the person using it?
choices: it must be impossible to open
exercises.explain: A lunch bag must hold a lunchbox; the other rules would make it worse to use.

exercises.prompt: Is it part of planning or making?
exercises.hint: Planning happens on paper; making uses the materials.
exercises.explain: Plan: sketch, list materials, choose tools. Make: measure and mark, cut, glue.

exercises.prompt: Match each step to what you do.
exercises.explain: Idea: think of many ways. Plan: draw and label. Make: cut and join. Test: check that it works.

exercises.prompt: If a design fails its test, you should give up.
exercises.hint: What is the next step of the cycle?
exercises.explain: False: a failed test shows what to improve. Change it and test again.

exercises.prompt: Mimi's paper bridge sags when a toy car crosses it. What should she do next?
exercises.hint: Change one thing, so you can tell what helped.
choices: fold the paper to stiffen it, then test again
exercises.explain: Change one thing (fold the paper to make it stiffer), then test again, so she knows what helped.

exercises.prompt: Bram made a pencil pot. How should he test it?
exercises.hint: What did the brief ask for?
choices: check it holds 10 pencils, as the brief asks
exercises.explain: A test checks the design against the brief, like holding 10 pencils without tipping over.

exercises.prompt: Why do designers sketch before they make?
exercises.hint: It is cheaper to fix a drawing than a model.
choices: to plan sizes and spot problems early
exercises.explain: A sketch plans sizes, materials and tools, and shows problems before anything is cut.

exercises.prompt: Put Zara's bird feeder project in order.
exercises.hint: Follow idea, plan, make, test, improve.
items: add a roof to keep the seeds dry
exercises.explain: Research, plan, make, test by watching, then improve (a roof keeps the seeds dry).

exercises.prompt: What does 'measure twice, cut once' mean?
choices: check a measurement before you cut
exercises.explain: Check your measurement again before cutting, because a cut cannot be undone.

exercises.prompt: The brief: a bag to carry a lunchbox for a child of 8. Sort the test results: meets the brief, or not?
items: it is too heavy to lift
its handle fits a child's hand
exercises.hint: Check each result against what the brief asks for.
exercises.explain: Meets it: it holds a lunchbox, a child can hold it and open it. Does not: too heavy, too small, and a strap that breaks. Those three show what to improve next.
